craft_claim: Superiority or mockery explains only part of humour and fails as comedy when the audience identifies with a non-benign target rather than with the mocker.

supporting_evidence.location: Argument against the sufficiency of superiority theory
supporting_evidence.note: Superiority theories capture a subset of humour and require refinement rather than serving as a general account.
Humour's influence on persuasion is small and condition-dependent, so comedy cannot be assumed to win assent or goodwill.

counterevidence.note: Superiority remains one of the three classical families and is a legitimate partial explanation of mockery-based humour.

scope: Humour aimed at persons or groups, and comic material used to persuade.
exceptions: Self-deprecating humour where the audience shares the narrator's position.
In-group humour that the in-group experiences as affiliative rather than diminishing.
